Abstract
Multiscale topology optimization (MSTO) enables the design of hierarchical structures with enhanced performance and 
complexity. However, solving nested optimization problems at multiple scales imposes high computational costs. This paper 
introduces a machine learning-based MSTO (ML-MSTO) framework that leverages displacement-driven topology-optimized 
microstructures (TOMs). An artificial neural network is trained to predict homogenized stiffness tensors of TOMs based on 
macroscale densities and nodal displacements. This surrogate model enables efficient macroscale outer-loop optimization 
by avoiding microscale inner-loop optimization. Sensitivities are computed analytically from the neural network’s Jacobian, 
eliminating the need for finite differences. The method is demonstrated on 2D and 3D benchmark problems, generating high-
fidelity, non-periodic multiscale structures with excellent compliance performance.

1  Introduction
Multiscale topology optimization (MSTO) enables the 
design of hierarchical, free-form structures that integrate 
macroscale and microscale features to achieve functionalities 
beyond the reach of conventional single-scale approaches. 
By embedding cellular microarchitectures within structural 
components, MSTO allows better control over mechanical 
behavior, weight distribution, and multifunctionality. These 
capabilities are particularly valuable in aerospace, automo-
tive, and biomedical applications, where performance cri-
teria such as energy absorption, thermal management, and 
material grading are relevant (Wu et al. 2021). The abil-
ity to spatially vary microstructural features makes MSTO 
amenable to additive manufacturing, enabling the fabrica-
tion of components with tailored porosity and anisotropic 
properties. However, these benefits come at the cost of sig-
nificantly increased computational demands and potential 
numerical intractability. Various MSTO formulations have 
been developed to address these challenges, each defined by 
its optimization strategy and the degree of design freedom 
allowed at the microscale.
1.1  State of the art
According to their optimization strategy, MSTO methods 
can be classified as single-loop or multiple-loop approaches. 
Single-loop methods optimize macroscale and microscale 
variables concurrently (Ypsilantis et al. 2022; Pizzolato 
et al. 2019) or directly solve for microscale design variables 
within a single optimization problem (Fujii et al. 2001). In 
contrast, multiple-loop methods decompose the problem into 
sequential or nested subproblems. Sequential approaches 
first optimize the macroscale design, then solve for the 
microscale variables (Liu et al. 2018). In contrast, nested 
approaches solve numerous inner microscale problems 
within each iteration of the outer macroscale optimization 
(Rodrigues et al. 2002).
According to the level of design freedom at the micro-
scale, MSTO methods can be categorized into those with 
restricted and unrestricted unit cells. Restricted unit-cell 
methods use pre-defined, parameterized geometries, such 
as rectangular holes (Bendsøe and Kikuchi 1988; Wu et al.

Recent studies have integrated machine learning (ML) 
into MSTO frameworks to better balance design freedom 
and computational cost. Most approaches use ML to predict 
microstructural mechanical properties using models such 
as artificial neural networks (ANNs) or Gaussian processes 
(GPs; White et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2020a). Others focus 
on generating microstructure topologies through generative 
models such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) or 
variational autoencoders (VAEs; Wang et al. 2020b; Seo 
and Min 2022).
Existing machine learning-based MSTO (ML-MSTO) 
methods using single-loop optimization typically rely on 
restricted unit-cell microstructures with pre-defined param-
eters. Most implementations employ ANNs to predict 
homogenized stiffness tensors based on parameters such as 
density (Watts et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2019, 2020a, b; Yilin 
et al. 2021), shape (Black and Najafi 2023), size (White et al. 
2019), or implicit surfaces (Zheng et al. 2021; Rastegarza-
deh et al. 2023). Other approaches use deep neural networks 
(DNNs) to generate microstructures parameterized by type, 
size, orientation, or their combinations (Wang et al. 2020a; 
Padhy et al. 2023; Chandrasekhar et al. 2022). The resulting 
microstructures typically include trusses (White et al. 2019; 
Watts et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2020a; Yilin et al. 2021; Chan-
drasekhar et al. 2023), functionally defined surfaces (Zhang 
et al. 2019, 2020a, b; Zheng et al. 2021; Rastegarzadeh et al. 
2023; Black and Najafi 2023), and micropillars (Padhy et al. 
2023). While these structured parameterizations simplify 
ML implementation by providing a well-defined design 
space, they inherently restrict the design freedom of the 
microstructures.
To overcome the limitations of restricted design freedom, 
several ML-MSTO methods adopt multiple-loop optimi-
zation strategies that generate microstructures by solving 
local optimization problems, such as inverse homogeniza-
tion (Wang et al. 2020b; Seo and Min 2022) or topology 
optimization (Patel et al. 2022). The approaches by Wang 
et al. (2020b) and Seo and Min (2022) leverage unrestricted 
unit-cell representations in the low-dimensional latent space 
during the macroscale optimization problem. The solution 
of nested optimization problems relies on models of locally 
optimized microstructures with GANs and VAEs. In con-
trast, the method proposed by Patel et al. (2022) employs a 
sequential optimization framework in which DNNs predict 
and refine microstructure connectivity based on the density 
and local displacements of a macroscale design obtained 
through modified Solid Isotropic Material with Penalization 
(SIMP) topology optimization.
1.2  Purpose
This work introduces a novel ML-MSTO method based on 
displacement-driven, topology-optimized microstructures 
(TOMs). The method employs a multiple-loop optimization 
framework that couples the macro and micro scales through 
machine learning-based homogenization models. The outer 
optimization problem is defined over the macroscale design 
domain, which is discretized into finite elements. Each finite 
element is associated with an inner density-based topol-
ogy optimization problem, where boundary conditions are 
derived from the element’s nodal displacements, and the 
volume fraction constraint is set by its local density. The 
resulting optimized microstructures define the TOMs. As 
a result, the TOMs are free-form and non-periodic, varying 
spatially in response to local macroscale densities and nodal 
displacements.
These macroscale densities and nodal displacements also 
serve as input features to train an artificial neural network 
(ANN) that predicts each TOM’s homogenized constitutive 
tensor. In doing so, the ANN replaces the need for iterative 
inner-loop topology optimization and numerical homogeni-
zation. Sensitivity analysis for the outer optimization is effi-
ciently approximated using the analytically derived Jacobian 
of the neural network (NNJ), enabling the use of a gradi-
ent-based optimization algorithm. Once the homogenized 
macroscale structure is optimized, a final set of TOMs is 
generated and assembled to reconstruct the complete mul-
tiscale design.
1.3  Related work
The proposed ML-MSTO method is similar to the multiple-
loop ML-MSTO framework developed by Patel et al. (2022). 
However, there are two key differences: (1) the neural net-
works in Patel et al. (2022) are used to generate microscale 
topologies rather than to predict homogenized stiffness ten-
sors, and (2) their optimization problems are solved sequen-
tially rather than hierarchically.
Because the present method uses neural networks to pre-
dict homogenized stiffness tensors, it also bears similarity to 
certain single-loop ML-MSTO methods (White et al. 2019; 
Watts et al. 2019; Yilin et al. 2021); however, a distinguish-
ing feature is the use of unrestricted unit-cell microstruc-
tures or TOMs. As a result, the proposed ML-MSTO method 
benefits from a simpler and more easily trained neural net-
work architecture, while retaining the flexibility to represent

1.4  Summary of contributions
The proposed ML-MSTO method makes two primary con-
tributions. First, it introduces a machine learning framework 
for predicting homogenized stiffness tensor properties of 
free-form, displacement-driven TOMs using a trained neural 
network. The network is trained on a large, augmented data-
set comprising eight million two-dimensional (2D) TOMs 
and 48 million three-dimensional (3D) TOMs. Both trained 
models and datasets are made publicly available in a GitHub 
repository (A). By replacing the need to solve inner optimi-
zation problems directly, the neural network enables efficient 
execution of the hierarchical optimization algorithm.
Second, the method approximates the sensitivity coef-
ficients for the macroscale objective function using the ana-
lytically derived neural network Jacobian (NNJ). This elimi-
nates the need for manually computing analytical derivatives 
or relying on computationally intensive numerical approxi-
mations such as finite differences (Najmon and Tovar 2024).
Although this paper focuses on minimum compliance 
problems, the proposed ML-MSTO framework is broadly 
applicable to other structural and multiphysics objectives. 
Its generality is supported by the NNJ-based sensitivity 
approximation, which eliminates the need for explicit sen-
sitivity coefficients.

2  Proposed ML‑MSTO
2.1  Overview
The proposed ML-MSTO method involves solving nested 
outer-loop and inner-loop optimization problems to deter-
mine the optimal material distribution at both the macroscale 
and microscale levels. However, explicitly solving the inner-
loop topology optimization for each finite element during 
every outer-loop iteration is computationally intractable for 
large-scale problems. To address this, the proposed method 
replaces the inner-loop optimization with a pre-trained 
ANN that predicts the homogenized constitutive tensors 
of the optimal microscale structures. This surrogate model 
eliminates the need for explicit microscale optimization 
and numerical homogenization (Andreassen and Andreasen 
2014) during the outer-loop iterations, which significantly 
reduces the overall computational cost.
While a traditional C1 interpolation can be employed, the 
use of ANNs is motivated by several practical considera-
tions. First, ANNs are universal function approximators that 
do not require an explicit basis function or kernel, making 
them particularly well-suited for mapping nodal displace-
ments and densities to locally homogenized orthotropic 
properties. Second, whereas traditional interpolators empha-
size exact fitting, ANNs are designed to balance approxi-
mation accuracy with generalization. This is especially

3  Microscale inner‑loop optimization 
and ANN development
To serve as a foundation for the microscale optimization 
problem, let us formulate a displacement-driven topology 
optimization problem. This formulation allows for several 
benefits in the microstructure design process. First, the for-
mulation addresses the open-ended question of defining a 
topology optimization problem for an arbitrary microstruc-
ture. Second, the formulation provides a general way to cou-
ple multiple scales. Lastly, the features of the formulation 
lend a convenient way to train ANNs to predict homogenized 
stiffness tensors. The resulting microstructure is referred to 
as topology-optimized microstructures (TOMs).
3.1  Topology‑optimized microstructures (TOMs)
Since microstructures are optimized for a given macroscale 
element, the boundary conditions, external loads, optimi-
zation function, and constraints of the inner optimization 
problem should be defined considering their relation to the 
overall macroscale structure. Additionally, the ability to 
represent a free-form microstructure with a few features is 
desirable since it enables greater computational tractability 
via ANNs. For these reasons, the definition of an inner opti-
mization problem should consider: (a) the response of the 
macroscale structure, (b) the ease of representation, (c) the 
objective function of the outer optimization problem, and (d) 
the relative density of the macroscale element.
The hierarchical structure of the ML-MSTO method 
requires that each inner-loop optimization problem be 
informed by the response of the overlying macroscale struc-
ture. Since the inner design domain 훺I is derived from a 
macroscale finite element domain 훺e , a natural approach is 
to use the field variables of element e (e.g., internal forces, 
displacements, temperatures) to define the boundary condi-
tions and loading for the corresponding inner optimization 
problem.
The microscale FEA model for inner-loop topology opti-
mization can be formulated using either prescribed trac-
tions or external forces (Neumann boundary conditions) 
in a force-driven formulation, or prescribed displacements 
(Dirichlet boundary conditions) in a displacement-driven 
formulation. Similar to the microstructures in Patel et al. 
(2022), the latter FEA model is implemented in this work 
for several reasons. First, a displacement-driven model can 
maintain better agreement between 훺I and the steady-state 
deformation of 훺e . Furthermore, the homogeneous boundary 
conditions of force-driven models would fix degrees of free-
dom (DOFs) of 훺I in a way that contradicts the steady-state 
deformation of 훺e . Second, the total number of supports 
and loads has the potential to be reduced in a displacement-
driven model since the prescribed displacements can induce 
a loading on the domain while also restricting DOFs to avoid 
matrix singularities. Reducing the number of supports and 
loads of boundary conditions lowers the total number of fea-
tures required to represent the inner optimization problem.

3.2  Local homogenization
Classical asymptotic homogenization assumes a periodic 
microstructure of an infinitely repeating unit cell (Kalam-
karov et al. 2009). Under this assumption, boundary con-
ditions such as periodic or affine Dirichlet conditions are 
defined to approximate the behavior of an infinite periodic 
medium and facilitate convergence to an effective contin-
uum. However, many practical multiscale structures, par-
ticularly those arising from topology optimization, do not 
exhibit periodicity across the macroscale design domain.
In this work, the topology-optimized microstructures 
(TOMs) are non-periodic and spatially adapted to the local 
macroscale design. Rather than enforcing periodicity, a local 
homogenization strategy is employed. In this formulation, 
each TOM is assigned inhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary 
conditions extracted from the macroscale nodal displace-
ment field. These displacement-driven boundary conditions 
ensure kinematic compatibility between adjacent micro-
structures and preserve physical consistency across the 
multiscale structure.
Homogenized constitutive tensors are computed using an 
energy-based numerical method. For 2D microstructures, the 
procedure described by Andreassen and Andreasen (2014) is 
used and extended to 3D cases. Although periodicity is not 
enforced, the concept of local homogenization assumes that 
each microstructure is locally representative of a smoothly 
varying material distribution. This approach remains valid 
provided that the gradients in geometry and material prop-
erties are small. Under such conditions, the effective stiff-
ness tensor obtained from the boundary-driven microstruc-
ture provides a close approximation to the true mechanical 
behavior in the neighborhood. Theoretical analyses and 
numerical studies have shown that the errors introduced by 
relaxing periodicity are small and acceptable in practical 
applications (Zhou and Li 2008; Garner et al. 2019; Jia et al. 
2020; Wang et al. 2022).
In the ML-MSTO framework, the homogenized stiffness 
tensors of TOMs are used both to train the artificial neu-
ral network (ANN) and to evaluate macroscale responses 
within the outer-loop optimization. These tensors reflect 
orthotropic behavior aligned with the local deformation 
field and enable efficient yet accurate coupling of micro-
scale design with macroscale performance. Despite the 
non-periodic nature of the TOMs, the resulting multiscale 
designs exhibit smooth global behavior and demonstrate the 
practical effectiveness of the local homogenization approach 
in topology optimization.

Data augmentation techniques are applicable since a given

scale topology. Unlike standard image augmentation tech-

orientation of the features must be completely preserved dur-

learning model. As such, data augmentation provides a very 
efficient way of increasing the dataset size and improves the 
models’ ability to predict an accurate constitutive tensor 
regardless of the orientation of a given TOM.
A data augmentation scheme is applied to the feature sets 
and the targets of the dataset. There are 7 orthogonal transfor-
mations for a 2D microstructure (Fig. 4) and 47 orthogonal 
transformations for a 3D microstructure. These transformations 
are physically interpreted as the unique topologies resulting 
from rotations and reflections of the original topology about 
the coordinate axes. The feature sets of these augmentations 
are found by performing the transformations on the spatially 
dependent features (e.g., boundary conditions) and not on the 
spatially independent features (e.g., target volume fraction). 
Likewise, the targets are found by performing the same orthog-
onal transformations on the homogenized constitutive tensors. 
By following the approach described by Slawinski (2003), the 
matrix representation of a fourth-order stiffness tensor can be

5  Numerical examples and evaluation
Following the ANN training (Sect. 3.5) and validation 
of the NNJ-based sensitivity analysis (Sect. 4.2), the 
ML-MSTO framework is applied to solve the minimum 
compliance problem on two benchmark examples: a two-
dimensional cantilever beam and a three-dimensional 
five-point bending plate. The setups for these problems 
are illustrated in Fig. 8. All outer-loop optimization prob-
lems are solved using the generalized optimality criterion 
method (GOCM), leveraging ANN-predicted stiffness 
tensors and NNJ-derived sensitivities. The remainder of 
this section evaluates the performance of key ML-MSTO 
parameters and demonstrates the framework’s ability to 
synthesize homogenized and dehomogenized multiscale 
structures.
5.1  Two‑dimensional cantilever beam
Three numerical studies are conducted using the 2D can-
tilever beam as a benchmark problem. The first study 
focuses on dehomogenization through explicit inner-loop 
topology optimization. Starting from a prescribed mac-
roscale density distribution, the algorithm generates the 
corresponding distribution of TOMs, resulting in a fully 
resolved multiscale structure. This case is evaluated with 
a grading parameter of 훿= 0 , corresponding to a fixed 
macroscale density field without outer-loop optimization.
The second study investigates the effects of key ML-
MSTO parameters, including the density grading param-
eter 훿 , the sensitivity filter radius rO , and the upper 
bounds on the admissible macroscale densities 훩ad . The 
third study builds on the insights from these parametric 
investigations and addresses the design of a large-scale 
multiscale cantilever beam featuring millions of elements 
and non-periodic, spatially graded microstructures. All 
optimization problems are subject to a volume fraction 
constraint of Vt = 0.5 , and the outer-loop optimization is 
carried out for a fixed number of 500 iterations.
5.1.1  Dehomogenization
The design domain for the 2D cantilever beam is discre-
tized into a 400 × 800 finite element mesh. As a reference, 
the minimum compliance problem is first solved using sin-
gle-scale topology optimization with the optimality crite-
rion (OC) method. The SIMP formulation is applied with 
a continuation scheme, in which the penalization power p 
is gradually increased from 1 to 3 following a sigmoidal 
progression (Fig. 9A). To match the resolution used by the 
TOMs, the sensitivity filter radius is set to rI = 2.5 elements.
Next, the ML-MSTO method is applied using a design 
domain 훺O discretized into 8 × 16 macroscale elements. 
Each macroscale element is associated with a 50 × 50 micro-
scale element mesh, resulting in a 400 × 800 element mesh 
upon dehomogenization via the explicit inner-loop optimi-
zation. To illustrate the dehomogenization procedure, all 
macroscale elements are initially assigned a uniform den-
sity value of 훩e = 0.5 , with no density grading constraint 
( 훿= 0 ). The resulting homogenized and dehomogenized 
structures are shown in Fig. 9B.
Finally, the macroscale density distribution 훩opt is 
obtained by solving the minimum compliance problem using 
SIMP with p = 1 and no filtering, corresponding to the var-
iable-thickness sheet formulation. The resulting multiscale 
structures, based on this optimized density distribution, are 
shown in Fig. 9C.
Within gray or porous regions of the macroscale design, 
the TOMs tend to exhibit truss-like features aligned with 
principal stress directions or load paths. These microstruc-

geometric continuity. This is facilitated by the prescribed 
nodal displacements, which act as kinematic connectivity 
constraints between adjacent TOMs (Zhou and Li 2008). 
However, regions with low macroscale density may produce 
disconnected or weakly connected TOMs after dehomog-
enization. Such connectivity issues can be mitigated using 
regularization strategies, including sensitivity filtering, den-
sity grading, and restrictions on the admissible macroscale 
density range. These strategies are discussed in Sect. 5.1.2.

modeling of homogenized properties, and a computa-
tionally efficient outer-loop optimization strategy. The 
core of the method is an artificial neural network (ANN) 
trained to predict the homogenized orthotropic stiffness 
tensors of non-periodic, topology-optimized microstruc-
tures (TOMs). These microstructures are generated via a 
displacement-driven, density-based topology optimization 
approach, where boundary conditions are derived from 
macroscale nodal displacements. The ANN replaces the 
need to iteratively solve expensive inner-loop optimization 
problems during the macroscale (outer-loop) design pro-
cess. Macroscale sensitivities are efficiently approximated 
using the neural network Jacobian (NNJ), which enables 
scalable gradient-based optimization.
After the outer-loop optimization converges, a final 
dehomogenization step is performed by solving explicit 
inner-loop topology optimization problems to reconstruct 
the full-resolution multiscale structure. This results in 
non-periodic microstructures that align with local mac-
roscale field variables (density and displacement), pro-
viding spatially graded, free-form architectures that help 
reduce directional bias and improve isotropy in mechanical 
performance.
To develop the ANN surrogate, initial datasets of 1 mil-
lion 2D and 3D TOMs were generated and augmented to 8 
million and 48 million samples, respectively. The trained 
models demonstrated high predictive accuracy ( R2 = 0.988 
for 2D and 0.998 for 3D), enabling robust performance 
across a wide range of macroscale conditions. While small 
approximation errors in the surrogate model can accumulate 
and introduce mild oscillations in convergence, these effects 
are manageable and are mitigated through sensitivity filter-
ing and density grading regularization.
The ML-MSTO framework was applied to two bench-
mark problems, a 2D cantilever beam and a 3D five-point 
bending plate, with final designs reaching up to 18 million 
and 7.8 million finite elements, respectively. The method 
successfully generated multiscale structures with fixed, 
density-graded, and infilled microstructures. While global 
connectivity is generally well preserved due to the kinematic 
formulation, some connectivity issues were observed, par-
ticularly in regions with low density or corner-only TOM 
connections. These limitations are being addressed through 
post-processing strategies to enhance manufacturability.
Although the current implementation is not intended to 
replace production-ready high-resolution methods such as 
single-scale SIMP with advanced solvers, the ML-MSTO 
framework provides a scalable alternative for early-stage 
multiscale design and design-space exploration. By eliminat-
ing the need to solve thousands of microscale optimization 
problems during the outer-loop phase, the method enables 
efficient generation of physically meaningful multiscale 
structures.
The framework is particularly well-suited for applica-
tions involving controlled porosity, lightweight structures, 
and functional gradation, especially in the context of addi-
tive manufacturing. The integration of machine learning and 
local homogenization allows for rapid conceptual design, 
and the spatial grading of TOMs introduces performance 
and architectural diversity that can inform further refine-
ment. Future work will extend the method to multiphysics 
problems and non-compliance objectives, building on the 
flexibility enabled by NNJ-based sensitivity approximations 
and data-driven surrogate modeling.

Abstract: Multiscale topology optimization (MSTO) enables the design of hierarchical structures with enhanced performance and complexity. However, solving nested optimization problems at multiple scales imposes high computational costs. This paper introduces a machine learning-based MSTO (ML-MSTO) framework that leverages displacement-driven topology-optimized microstructures (TOMs). An artificial neural network is trained to predict homogenized stiffness tensors of TOMs based on macroscale densities and nodal displacements. This surrogate model enables efficient macroscale outer-loop optimization by avoiding microscale inner-loop optimization. Sensitivities are computed analytically from the neural network’s Jacobian, eliminating the need for finite differences. The method is demonstrated on 2D and 3D benchmark problems, generating high- fidelity, non-periodic multiscale structures with excellent compliance performance.
